stem: A support agent handles long multi-turn conversations. Over time, the running summary condenses the order total ($1,249.00), the order date, and the RMA number into vague phrases like "a recent high-value order." The agent then quotes wrong figures. What is the most reliable fix?

options.A: Extract transactional facts into a persistent case-facts block sent with every prompt, outside the summarized history
options.B: Disable summarization entirely and pass the full raw history on every turn so nothing is ever condensed
options.C: Instruct the model in its system prompt never to summarize numeric values, dates, or identifiers
options.D: Raise max_tokens so the running summary has room to retain the original figures verbatim

explanation: Progressive summarization reliably degrades precise transactional data. A case-facts block holds the amounts, dates, order/RMA numbers and statuses verbatim in a structured block that travels with each prompt OUTSIDE the summarized history (A), so compression can never reach them.

distractors.B: Never summarizing eventually overflows the context window in a long conversation; the goal is to keep the facts that matter, not every raw turn.
distractors.C: A prompt instruction is probabilistic and decays over many turns; it does not guarantee the values survive compression.
distractors.D: max_tokens caps Claude's output length, not whether summarization drops precise figures from the running history.

stem: A synthesis agent receives a single long concatenation of findings from five subagents. It consistently captures conclusions from the first and last subagents but omits findings from those in the middle. What is the best mitigation?

options.A: Increase the model's temperature so it samples more widely across the input it was given
options.B: Truncate the input to the first and last subagents' findings, where the model already attends reliably
options.C: Place a key-findings summary at the top and split the details under explicit per-subagent headers
options.D: Process the concatenation in reverse order so the previously omitted middle is read last

explanation: This is the "lost in the middle" effect: models reliably attend to the beginning and end of long inputs but may skip middle content. A key-findings summary up front plus explicit section headers (C) makes the middle salient and individually addressable rather than relying on position alone.

distractors.A: Temperature controls output randomness, not how attention is distributed across a long input.
distractors.B: Restricting the input to the positions the model already reads well deliberately discards exactly the findings being lost.
distractors.D: Reversing the order just moves the neglected content to a new middle position; the positional bias travels with it.

stem: A customer's first message is: "Stop wasting my time with bots. I want to speak to a human, now." The requested action (checking an order status) is something the agent can easily do. What should the agent do?

options.A: Acknowledge the frustration, attempt resolution, and escalate only if frustration persists
options.B: Investigate and resolve the order question first, then escalate only if the customer asks again
options.C: Escalate to a human immediately, without first attempting to investigate or resolve
options.D: Ask the customer why they want a human before deciding whether escalation is warranted

explanation: An explicit request for a human is a hard escalation trigger: escalate immediately, with no investigation first (C). The agent should not gate an explicit human request behind a resolution attempt or an interrogation, however easily it could have handled the underlying task.

distractors.A: Offering resolution first is the right response to implicit frustration alone, not to an explicit demand for a human.
distractors.B: Resolving first applies to implicit frustration; here it delays a direct instruction the customer already gave.
distractors.D: Asking the customer to justify the request adds friction and still ignores an explicit, unambiguous instruction.

stem: An order lookup tool returns 40+ fields per order, but only 5 are relevant to return processing. Across a long conversation these full payloads accumulate and crowd out context. What is the recommended approach?

options.A: Switch to a model with a larger context window so the full payloads fit comfortably
options.B: Ask the customer to read the relevant order details aloud so the agent can skip the tool call
options.C: Trim the tool output to only the fields return processing needs before it enters the context
options.D: Raise max_tokens so the extra fields have room and stop crowding out the rest of the conversation

explanation: Verbose tool outputs cause context bloat: 35 of the 40 fields are dead weight on every call, and they accumulate turn after turn. Trimming the payload to the five relevant fields before it ever enters the conversation (C) is the mitigation that keeps context lean across a long session.

distractors.A: A bigger window delays the problem and raises cost; the 35 irrelevant fields per call still accumulate.
distractors.B: Routing data through the customer is slow and error-prone when the tool already returns it reliably.
distractors.D: max_tokens governs the length of Claude's output, not the size of tool results accumulating in context.

stem: During a long codebase-exploration session, Claude Code starts giving inconsistent answers and refers to "typical patterns" rather than the specific classes it identified earlier. The verbose discovery output has filled the context. What is the most appropriate first action?

options.A: Restart from scratch in a brand-new session and re-explore the codebase
options.B: Ask the same questions repeatedly until the answers stabilize on a consistent picture
options.C: Run /compact to condense the filled context and continue in the same session
options.D: Raise the temperature so the model produces more varied, less repetitive answers

explanation: When context fills with verbose discovery output and answers degrade into generalities, /compact condenses the conversation in place (C) so the session continues with the important information retained. It targets the bloat that is actually causing the degradation, at the lowest cost of the four.

distractors.A: A full restart throws away every finding from the exploration and pays to rediscover all of it.
distractors.B: Re-asking reclaims no context space, so the answers stay generic — the bloat causing them is untouched.
distractors.D: Higher temperature increases variability, which makes the inconsistency worse rather than better.

stem: A customer provides only a common name, "John Smith." The get_customer tool returns three distinct accounts matching that name. What should the agent do before taking any account action?

options.A: Ask the customer for an email, order number, or account ID that disambiguates the three matches
options.B: Pick the account with the most recent activity, since that is the likeliest to be the current customer
options.C: Act on all three accounts in parallel and let the customer flag whichever one was not theirs
options.D: Pick the account whose city best matches the customer's IP geolocation and proceed with that one

explanation: When a lookup returns multiple customer matches, the agent should request an additional identifier and disambiguate (A) before taking any account action. Every alternative substitutes a heuristic guess for identity verification, and the cost of guessing wrong is action on another person's account.

distractors.B: "Most recent activity" is a heuristic that can easily select the wrong John Smith, and nothing in the conversation supports it.
distractors.C: Acting on all three accounts risks exposing or modifying two other customers' data before anyone can object.
distractors.D: IP geolocation is unreliable at city granularity and is not identity evidence; it can act on the wrong account.

stem: A document-analysis subagent fails on 2 of 5 documents (one timeout, one parse error) but succeeds on 3. Its current behavior is to return an empty result set marked as successful so the workflow does not halt. Why is this the wrong design?

options.A: It should terminate the entire workflow immediately so a human can intervene before synthesis
options.B: It should retry the two failed documents indefinitely until both eventually parse successfully
options.C: It is correct — an empty success keeps the pipeline running and the coordinator can detect the gap
options.D: It silently suppresses errors and drops the partial results, hiding both from the coordinator

explanation: Returning empty results marked as success is the silent-suppression anti-pattern (D): the coordinator cannot tell that 2 documents failed, nor that 3 succeeded, so downstream synthesis treats incomplete data as complete. The subagent should return structured error context — failure type per document — alongside the 3 partial results.

distractors.A: Terminating the whole workflow on a partial failure discards the 3 successful analyses and over-reacts to a recoverable problem.
distractors.B: Unbounded retries can hang the pipeline, and a parse error on a malformed document will never resolve itself.
distractors.C: Empty-as-success gives the coordinator nothing to detect — an empty set is indistinguishable from a genuine zero-result run.

stem: A web-search subagent hits a transient timeout, then propagates {"status": "error", "message": "search unavailable"} to the coordinator. The coordinator blindly retries the same query, which times out again. What two problems does this reveal?

options.A: The subagent should average across whatever data it did retrieve and report the call as a success
options.B: The coordinator should never retry a failed search, and the subagent should escalate straight to a human
options.C: The failure should have been raised as a JSON-RPC protocol error, which the coordinator can safely ignore
options.D: Recover transient failures inside the subagent, and give any propagated error structured context

explanation: Two issues (D). First, a transient timeout should be handled by local recovery inside the subagent before it is propagated at all. Second, an error that does reach the coordinator must carry structured context — failure type, the query attempted, any partial results, and viable alternatives — so the coordinator can choose a different query or source instead of blindly resending the one that just failed.

distractors.A: Fabricating a success from incomplete data is the silent-suppression anti-pattern; the coordinator would never learn the search failed.
distractors.B: Retries are appropriate for transient faults given the right context; jumping straight to a human on a timeout is premature.
distractors.C: Tool and agent failures belong in readable error context the coordinator can reason over, not buried in a protocol error it ignores.

stem: A coordinator must distinguish between a search tool that timed out and a search tool that completed successfully but found zero matching records. Why does this distinction matter for reliability?

options.A: A timeout is an unresolved access failure that may warrant a retry, while a zero-result response is correct data
options.B: Both should be reported as empty successes so the coordinator's handling stays simple and uniform
options.C: Only the empty result needs special handling; a timeout can be ignored and the query treated as done
options.D: It does not matter — both mean no data came back, so both should be retried the same way

explanation: An access failure (timeout, service down) is unresolved and may warrant a retry; a valid empty result is a successful query that genuinely found nothing (A). Conflating them either wastes retries on real zero-result answers or silently drops real failures, so error reporting must keep the two distinguishable at the coordinator.

distractors.B: Reporting a timeout as an empty success hides a real failure and makes an unanswered question look answered.
distractors.C: Ignoring timeouts lets real access failures pass silently into the results as though the source had been checked.
distractors.D: Retrying a genuine zero-result query burns budget on a call that can only ever return the same correct answer.

stem: A final research report states "Battery storage costs fell 76% over the last decade" with no source. The synthesis step compressed findings and dropped the source URLs, excerpts, and dates from the subagents. What design change best prevents this loss of provenance?

options.A: Have the synthesis agent re-search each claim afterwards and attach whatever source it then finds
options.B: Append a generic bibliography listing every URL any subagent visited at the end of the report
options.C: Require subagents to emit structured claim-source mappings that synthesis is required to preserve
options.D: Instruct the synthesis agent to include only the claims it is confident it can stand behind

explanation: Provenance is lost when findings are compressed without preserving the claim-to-source link. Requiring subagents to emit structured claim-source mappings (C) — source URL or document, the relevant excerpt, and the publication or collection date — and treating those mappings as data synthesis must carry through keeps each statistic traceable instead of reconstructed after the fact.

distractors.A: Re-searching after the fact is unreliable and may attach a different source than the one that actually produced the claim.
distractors.B: A bulk bibliography does not map a specific claim to a specific source, so the 76% figure remains unverifiable.
distractors.D: Confidence filtering removes some claims but restores no attribution for the ones that survive.

stem: Two sources report a key figure differently: one says "45% growth (2022 data)" and another says "52% growth (2024 data)." The synthesis agent must decide how to present this. What is the correct approach?

options.A: Silently keep the higher figure, on the grounds that the more recent 2024 collection supersedes the older
options.B: Report both figures with their sources and dates, flagging the conflict for the reader to reconcile
options.C: Drop both figures because they conflict, and report only that growth occurred over the period
options.D: Average the two figures and report a single 48.5% growth rate to avoid confusing the reader

explanation: Conflicting source values should be annotated with their attribution and dates rather than resolved by a silent heuristic (B). Preserving the dates also prevents a temporal difference — 2022 data versus 2024 data — from being read as a contradiction at all. The reconciliation decision belongs to the coordinator or reader, who can see both.

distractors.A: Picking one value silently discards provenance and hides a difference the reader needs to see to judge either figure.
distractors.C: Dropping both throws away two genuine, datable data points to avoid a conflict that annotation would resolve.
distractors.D: Averaging fabricates a number neither source reported and erases the temporal distinction between them.

stem: You explored a large codebase yesterday and built up significant findings in the session. Overnight, three specific files were modified by teammates. You want to continue the investigation today. What is the best approach?

options.A: Start a fresh session and re-explore the whole codebase so nothing carried over can be stale
options.B: Resume with --resume and tell the agent which three files changed so it re-analyzes them
options.C: Resume with --resume and let the agent rediscover the overnight changes as it works
options.D: Start a fresh session, since a resumed session always reasons over stale cached tool results

explanation: When prior context is mostly still valid but a few files changed, resume with --resume AND name the three changed files (B) so the agent re-analyzes exactly those. That preserves yesterday's valid findings while preventing the agent from reasoning over stale tool results for the files that moved underneath it.

distractors.A: Re-exploring everything discards a large body of still-valid work to correct three files.
distractors.C: Without being told, the agent has no reason to re-read those files and may keep using yesterday's cached results.
distractors.D: Resuming is appropriate when most context is valid; a fresh start is only warranted when prior results are extensively stale.

stem: During a long, multi-phase codebase exploration you are worried key findings from early phases will be lost as the session grows. Which combination best preserves them across context boundaries?

options.A: Write findings to scratchpad files, delegate narrow questions to subagents, and seed each phase with the last summary
options.B: Switch to a model with a larger context window and disable compaction so nothing is ever condensed
options.C: Keep everything in the one conversation and rely on the model recalling the earlier phases accurately
options.D: Restart the session between phases so each phase begins with a clean, uncluttered context

explanation: The recommended pattern combines three moves (A): externalize findings into scratchpad files the agent can re-read, delegate narrow questions to subagents so their verbose output never lands in the main context, and summarize each phase's key findings into the initial context of the next. Together they keep durable knowledge available across context boundaries.

distractors.B: A larger window still fills and still degrades; without externalized findings, the early phases are lost just the same.
distractors.C: In-context recall over many phases is exactly what fails here — it is the mechanism the question is asking you to replace.
distractors.D: Restarting clears the clutter but also drops cross-phase continuity, unless findings are carried forward some other way.

stem: A team wants the agent to auto-escalate cases it is unsure about. A proposal is to have the model output a self-reported confidence score per case and escalate when it falls below a threshold. Why is this routing signal unreliable?

options.A: Confidence scores trend high across the board, so the escalation threshold simply needs raising
options.B: Confidence scores are calibrated for extraction tasks only and do not transfer to a support routing decision
options.C: Computing a confidence score for every case is too expensive to run at the team's ticket volume
options.D: Self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated — models are often confidently wrong on the hard cases

explanation: Self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated: a model can be highly confident and wrong, and it is most likely to be so on difficult cases — the very ones the threshold is meant to catch (D). Routing on this signal lets hard, confidently-wrong cases through. An independent review or verification pass is a more reliable trigger than the model grading itself.

distractors.A: The failure is not a uniform offset a higher threshold would correct; the score does not track correctness at all.
distractors.B: Poor calibration of self-reported confidence is a general property of the signal, not a quirk of support routing.
distractors.C: The score is one extra token per case, so cost is not the objection; calibration is.

stem: An extraction pipeline reports 97% overall accuracy on a labeled set, so the team proposes turning off human review entirely. What is the strongest objection?

options.A: Accuracy should be re-measured at a higher temperature before any change to review is made
options.B: The model should self-report confidence per item and route the low-confidence ones, replacing validation
options.C: 97% clears the bar the team set, so human review can be removed across all document types now
options.D: Aggregate accuracy can mask segment-level failures, so validate stratified by document type and field

explanation: A high aggregate can hide a segment performing far worse — one document type, or one field across all types. Before reducing human review, validate accuracy stratified by document type AND by field (D) to confirm the number holds everywhere, not just on average across a mix dominated by easy documents.

distractors.A: Temperature has no bearing on whether an aggregate figure conceals a failing segment beneath it.
distractors.B: Self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated and cannot substitute for measuring accuracy against labels.
distractors.C: Acting on the aggregate alone is precisely the trap: the 3% may be concentrated in one document type.

stem: An extraction call fails a semantic check: the line items do not sum to the stated invoice total (the JSON is syntactically valid). You implement retry-with-error-feedback that resends the document, the failed extraction, and the specific validation error. What additional safeguard is most important?

options.A: Bound the retries and, once the bound is exhausted, route the item to human review with the error context
options.B: Escalate to a larger, more capable model once an item has failed validation 50 consecutive times
options.C: Allow unlimited retries with error feedback so every extraction is resent until it validates
options.D: Drop the sum check and accept any syntactically valid JSON the extraction call returns

explanation: Retry-with-error-feedback must be bounded (A). Some documents will never validate — the source invoice may genuinely not sum — so unbounded retries burn cost and can loop forever on an unwinnable item. When the bound is hit, hand the item to a human with the captured validation error so the reviewer starts from the diagnosis rather than from scratch.

distractors.B: A 50-failure threshold is effectively unbounded per item, and a larger model cannot reconcile a document that is internally inconsistent.
distractors.C: Unlimited retries loop indefinitely on inputs that can never satisfy the check, and nothing ever reaches a human.
distractors.D: Removing the check makes every extraction "succeed" while letting genuinely wrong totals through — the opposite of reliability.

stem: A research synthesis must produce a report when one subagent's source domain was unreachable, so that subtopic has thin coverage while others are well-supported. The coordinator's instinct is to abort the whole report. What is the most reliable behavior?

options.A: Continue with the partial results and annotate which subtopics are well-supported and which have gaps
options.B: Fill the thin subtopic from the model's own general knowledge so the report reads as complete
options.C: Abort the report entirely, since one thinly-sourced subtopic makes the whole thing untrustworthy
options.D: Replace the missing subtopic with findings duplicated from a better-covered subtopic

explanation: Graceful degradation: one unreachable source should not terminate a workflow that succeeded everywhere else. Continue with the partial results and annotate coverage (A), distinguishing well-supported findings from the subtopic left thin by an unavailable source, so the report stays honest and still useful to the reader.

distractors.B: Backfilling from general knowledge fabricates coverage and gives the reader no way to tell sourced findings from invented ones.
distractors.C: Terminating on a single source failure discards substantial valid work and is the anti-pattern graceful degradation exists to avoid.
distractors.D: Copying findings from a different subtopic misrepresents what was actually researched about the missing one.

stem: Downstream agents in your pipeline have small context budgets. A research subagent currently returns long prose with its full reasoning chain, overflowing those budgets. How should the subagent's output be redesigned, and how should the final report render mixed content?

options.A: Return the raw tool outputs unchanged and let each downstream agent trim them to fit its own context budget
options.B: Return the full prose and reasoning chain verbatim, and convert the entire report to a single uniform format
options.C: Return compact structured findings with citations and metadata, rendering each type in its natural form
options.D: Return a one-sentence summary with no metadata, and render the whole report as a flat bullet list

explanation: With small downstream budgets, subagents should return compact structured data — key facts, citations, relevance scores, and required metadata such as dates and source locations — rather than prose and reasoning chains (C). The final report should then render each content type in its natural form: financial data as tables, news as prose, technical findings as structured lists, instead of flattening everything into one format.

distractors.A: Pushing the trimming downstream still spends each agent's scarce budget receiving the bloat before it can discard it.
distractors.B: Verbatim prose overflows the small budgets the stem describes, and one uniform format misrepresents tabular and narrative content alike.
distractors.D: Stripping metadata destroys the provenance downstream agents need, and a flat bullet list is the wrong shape for financial tables.

stem: Your support agent resolves only 55% of issues against a target of 80%. Analysis shows miscalibration in both directions: it escalates simple cases a human should not need to see, yet attempts to handle complex policy exceptions autonomously. How do you improve its escalation calibration?

options.A: Add explicit escalation criteria to the prompt, with few-shot examples of cases on each side
options.B: Have the model self-rate its confidence 1-10 per case and escalate automatically below a threshold
options.C: Train a separate classifier on historical ticket data and let it make the escalation decision
options.D: Run sentiment analysis on the customer's messages and escalate whenever the tone turns negative

explanation: Miscalibration in both directions points to one root cause: the decision boundary was never stated. Explicit escalation criteria paired with few-shot examples of cases on each side (A) teach that boundary directly, which fixes the over-escalation of simple cases and the over-confidence on policy exceptions at the same time.

distractors.B: LLM self-rated confidence is poorly calibrated — the model is confidently wrong on exactly the complex policy cases that should escalate.
distractors.C: Training a classifier is heavy engineering for a problem whose cause is that nobody ever wrote the boundary down.
distractors.D: Sentiment measures mood, not complexity: an angry customer may have a trivial issue and a calm one a genuine policy exception.

stem: Your document-analysis subagent encounters a corrupted PDF file that it cannot parse. When designing the system's error handling, what is the most effective way to handle this failure?

options.A: Return an error with context to the coordinator agent, allowing it to decide how to proceed
options.B: Silently skip the corrupted document and continue with the remaining files so the workflow is not interrupted
options.C: Automatically retry parsing the document three times with exponential backoff before reporting a failure
options.D: Throw an exception that terminates the entire research workflow so the corruption cannot be missed

explanation: Returning a structured error with context to the coordinator (A) lets it make an informed decision — skip the file, try an alternative parser, or notify the user — while keeping full visibility of the failure. The subagent's job is to report accurately; the routing decision belongs one level up.

distractors.B: Silently skipping hides the failure, so the final output looks complete when a source document was never analyzed.
distractors.C: File corruption is deterministic, not transient; three backed-off retries spend time on a failure that cannot resolve itself.
distractors.D: One unparseable file should not kill the workflow and discard every other document's valid progress.

stem: After calling `get_customer` and `lookup_order`, your support agent has all available system data but still faces uncertainty. Which situation is the most justified trigger for calling `escalate_to_human`?

options.A: An order shipped yesterday arrives tomorrow and the customer wants it cancelled — escalate, since they may change their mind
options.B: A customer denies receiving an order that tracking shows delivered and signed for — escalate rather than contradict them
options.C: A customer asks for competitor price matching; your policy covers only price drops on your own site — escalate for interpretation
options.D: One message contains both a billing question and a return — escalate so a human can coordinate the two together

explanation: Competitor price matching is a genuine policy gap (C): the documented rules cover price drops on the company's own site within 14 days and say nothing about competitors. An agent must never invent or extend policy, so interpreting a rule that does not exist is exactly the judgment call that belongs with a human.

distractors.A: Cancelling a shipped order is a standard operational case covered by existing policy; speculation about a future change of mind is not an escalation criterion.
distractors.B: Tracking data directly answers the claim, and presenting documented evidence is within the agent's capability; an uncomfortable conversation is not a policy gap.
distractors.D: Handling several issues in one interaction is exactly what decomposition is for; a multi-part request alone does not require a human.

stem: Over several turns discussing investment strategy, a user stated "I have a very low risk tolerance" and later "I want to maximize my returns." They now ask: "What should I invest in?" Which approach best ensures the recommendation aligns with the user's actual priority?

options.A: Surface the contradiction between the two stated preferences and ask which one should govern.
options.B: Give two separate recommendations, one built for each of the two preferences the user has stated.
options.C: Proceed using the most recently stated preference, treating it as the governing one.
options.D: Recommend a balanced portfolio that splits the difference without raising the conflict.

explanation: Low risk tolerance and maximizing returns are fundamentally incompatible goals. When stated preferences directly contradict each other, surfacing the conflict and asking which one governs (A) is the only approach that does not substitute an assumption for the user's actual priority.

distractors.B: Two parallel recommendations dodge the decision and hand the unresolved contradiction back without even naming it.
distractors.C: Recency is an arbitrary tiebreaker — the user never retracted the risk constraint, so the later statement is not evidence of priority.
distractors.D: A balanced portfolio silently substitutes the assistant's compromise for the user's unknown priority and hides that a conflict exists.

stem: In your playlist assistant, users refine their preferences over multiple conversation turns. Two messages after a user said "I love jazz," Claude asks "What genres do you enjoy?" What is the most likely cause?

options.A: Claude requires a vector database connection to maintain conversation memory, and none is configured.
options.B: The model's context window has been exceeded, so the earliest turns were silently dropped.
options.C: The Claude API requires a `session_id` parameter to link requests, which your application is not sending.
options.D: Your application is not including prior turns in the `messages` array of each API request.

explanation: The Claude API is stateless — it holds no server-side memory of previous calls. Every request must carry the full conversation history in the `messages` array (D); if the application sends only the latest message, Claude has no knowledge of anything said earlier, including "I love jazz" two turns ago.

distractors.A: Claude has no vector-database dependency; conversation memory is simply whatever the caller chooses to include in the request.
distractors.B: A two-message exchange is nowhere near any context-window limit, so truncation cannot explain the loss.
distractors.C: The Messages API has no `session_id` parameter; maintaining conversation state is entirely the application's responsibility.

stem: After a 40-minute cooking-assistant session, the conversation reaches 78,000 tokens. The history includes the user's allergies, recipe scaling calculations, clarified cooking terms, and general discussion. You must reduce token usage while preserving important information. Which approach best balances preservation with token reduction?

options.A: Summarize the entire conversation history into a single condensed narrative of the session.
options.B: Keep only the most recent 20,000 tokens of history and drop everything stated before that.
options.C: Extract the critical facts into a compact block, summarize the general discussion, keep recent turns verbatim.
options.D: Store the full conversation externally and retrieve the relevant parts by semantic search on each turn.

explanation: The hybrid approach preserves the highest-value information at the lowest token cost (C): safety-critical precise facts — allergies, quantities, preferences — go into a compact structured block immune to summarization's precision loss; low-value general discussion is compressed; and recent exchanges stay verbatim so the conversation still reads coherently.

distractors.A: Whole-history summarization compresses allergies and scaling factors into lossy prose — exactly the data that has to survive exactly.
distractors.B: A pure recency window silently discards the allergy and recipe-scaling information stated early in the session.
distractors.D: External storage with per-turn retrieval is architectural overkill for one session, and retrieval can miss a critical fact that is not semantically close to the current question.

stem: Users of your conversational assistant report that latency increases and costs rise as conversations exceed 50 turns. What is the primary cause?

options.A: The full conversation history is sent with every request, so input tokens grow with each turn.
options.B: The model generates progressively longer responses as the conversation continues past 50 turns.
options.C: Database operations slow down as the stored conversation history grows larger over time.
options.D: The model builds an internal user profile that costs progressively more to process as it grows.

explanation: Claude's API is stateless — each request must include the complete conversation history in the `messages` array (A). As the conversation grows, every request carries more input tokens, which raises both processing latency and per-request cost, and the growth is linear in turns.

distractors.B: Response length is driven by the request and its content, not by how old the conversation is.
distractors.C: Application database latency is independent of the model API and would not explain rising token costs.
distractors.D: The API is stateless; the model keeps no internal profile or other state between calls.

stem: Your book-club assistant has accumulated 85,000 tokens of conversation history over three months of weekly sessions. When a user asks "What did we conclude about the theme of isolation?", the assistant gives generic answers instead of referencing the previous discussions. What is the most effective approach?

options.A: Apply rolling-window truncation so only the most recent weekly sessions stay in context.
options.B: Use progressive summarization that captures each session's key conclusions as the session ends.
options.C: Index the history with semantic embeddings and retrieve the relevant past exchanges on demand.
options.D: Add structured XML tags marking each session's discussion conclusions throughout the stored history.

explanation: Semantic retrieval over the archived history (C) is the only option that scales to three months of discussion while still surfacing the specific exchange a question refers to. The conclusion about isolation can be located and injected on demand, restoring the specificity the generic answers lack.

distractors.A: Truncation discards exactly the months-old sessions the user is asking about.
distractors.B: Summarization compresses specific conclusions into abstractions, so the generic-answer problem returns in another form.
distractors.D: Tagging requires restructuring all past content and still leaves 85,000 tokens that must be fitted or searched at question time.

stem: During QA testing, Claude follows your system-prompt guidelines for the first 10-15 turns of a conversation, but later responses begin to deviate. The conversation is still well within token limits. What is the best solution?

options.A: Move the behavioral guidelines out of the system prompt and into the first user message instead.
options.B: Automatically start a new conversation after 20 turns so the guidelines stay dominant.
options.C: Insert user-role messages that reinforce the guidelines at natural conversation breakpoints.
options.D: Use post-response validation that detects non-compliant responses and regenerates them.

explanation: Periodic reinforcement directly counters instruction drift (C): as history accumulates and dilutes the system prompt's influence, re-injecting the guidelines at natural breakpoints re-establishes the constraints without discarding the conversation. It is preventive, cheap, and leaves the context intact.

distractors.A: A first user message carries less persistent authority than the system prompt and drifts into the middle of the context just as fast.
distractors.B: Resetting every 20 turns destroys accumulated context and degrades the experience to fix what an in-place reminder solves.
distractors.D: Regeneration is corrective rather than preventive, adds latency and cost per violation, and needs a reliable compliance detector of its own.

stem: Users of your event-planning assistant frequently send requests like "Book a venue for the party." The assistant responds with four or more clarifying questions, and 35% of users abandon the conversation. What approach best improves the clarification-versus-friction trade-off?

options.A: Proceed immediately using hidden default values for every detail of the booking the user left unspecified
options.B: Ask all four clarifying questions at once in a single compound message at the start of the conversation
options.C: State reasonable assumptions explicitly, proceed with them, and invite the user to correct any.
options.D: Replace the conversation with a structured intake form that collects every required detail up front

explanation: Stating assumptions explicitly and proceeding (C) gives the user an immediately useful response — removing the friction that drives the 35% abandonment — while keeping them informed and in control, because any wrong assumption is visible on the page and trivially correctable.

distractors.A: Hidden defaults produce a result the user cannot sanity-check; they never learn what was assumed, so errors surface late.
distractors.B: A wall of questions still demands the same upfront effort that is driving abandonment, merely compressed into one message.
distractors.D: A form adds more upfront friction than the questions did, pushing directly against the abandonment problem.

stem: Your assistant uses a contractor-persona system prompt. Early turns follow the persona rules, but by turn 7 the assistant is giving generic advice. The whole conversation is only about 2,500 tokens. What is the most likely cause?

options.A: System prompts establish only the initial behavior and stop applying once the conversation is underway.
options.B: The model's attention mechanism weakens as more conversation turns accumulate in the context window.
options.C: Accumulated assistant responses dilute the system prompt as the model pattern-matches its own output.
options.D: The system prompt is sent only on the first API call and is absent from every later request.

explanation: As assistant responses accumulate, the share of context reflecting the system prompt's constraints shrinks against the model's own generated content (C). The model increasingly pattern-matches to its prior outputs, so a slight drift toward generic advice compounds — which is why the persona decays even at only 2,500 tokens.

distractors.A: System prompts apply to the whole conversation on every request; there is no built-in expiry after early turns.
distractors.B: Attention-related degradation is a long-context phenomenon and cannot explain drift at 2,500 tokens.
distractors.D: A correct integration sends the system prompt on every call, and a genuinely missing prompt would cause an abrupt break, not gradual drift.

stem: An analytics team wants a nightly job that summarizes and categorizes the day's ~8,000 closed support transcripts to populate a quality dashboard that reviewers open the next morning. They are deciding whether to route this workload through the asynchronous Message Batches API instead of the synchronous Messages API. Select the TWO signs that indicate this workload is a good fit for the Message Batches API.

options.A: The results are not needed until the next morning, so no user is blocked waiting on them
options.B: The job processes thousands of independent records in bulk rather than one request at a time
options.C: Each transcript must be categorized at the lowest possible per-request latency the API allows
options.D: The categorization output must stream token-by-token into a live reviewer UI as it is produced

explanation: The Message Batches API is asynchronous, with a processing window of up to 24 hours, and roughly 50% cheaper — which fits bulk, non-time-sensitive work. The deciding question is whether the workflow blocks: here nobody waits on the results until morning (A), and it is a large volume of independent requests run for throughput and cost rather than interactivity (B).

distractors.C: A requirement for the lowest possible per-request latency is an interactive signal pointing at the synchronous Messages API, which is what batch trades away.
distractors.D: Streaming into a live UI needs a blocking synchronous request; batch results return asynchronously and cannot feed a token-by-token view.

stem: Your agent calls an issue_refund tool. Intermittently the call times out or returns HTTP 503 with no body, so the agent retries it. Some customers then receive two refunds, because the original request had actually succeeded but its response was lost in transit. What is the most reliable fix?

options.A: Add a fixed 5-second delay before every refund call so the payment service is never overloaded
options.B: Send each refund with a unique idempotency key so the payment service deduplicates the retry
options.C: Stop retrying refund calls and escalate every timeout or 503 to a human for manual issue
options.D: Have the model track which customers it has already refunded in this conversation and skip them

explanation: Timeouts and 503s are transient and safe to retry, but issue_refund has a side effect, so a retry can execute the refund a second time when only the response was lost. An idempotency key (B) lets the payment service recognize the retry as the same logical operation and return the original result instead of issuing a duplicate — the deterministic fix that makes retry-with-backoff safe for non-idempotent actions.

distractors.A: A fixed delay treats the wrong cause; it does nothing to stop a retry from re-executing a refund that already succeeded.
distractors.C: Abandoning retries over-reacts to a routinely retryable error and dumps automatable work on humans; idempotency solves the duplicate, not giving up.
distractors.D: Model memory is a probabilistic substitute for a deterministic guarantee and does not survive a crash, a new session, or parallel agents.

stem: To cut human review, your extraction pipeline asks the model to emit a self-reported confidence score for each field and auto-approves anything scoring above 0.9. Spot checks reveal a steady stream of confidently wrong values sitting well above that threshold. What is the core problem, and the right fix?

options.A: Self-reported confidence is not calibrated; measure precision against labeled outcomes and set the cutoff there.
options.B: The threshold is simply too permissive; raise it to 0.99 and auto-approve everything above that line.
options.C: The model lacks context to judge its own output; enlarge the context window so the scores become trustworthy.
options.D: Self-reported confidence is unusable in principle, so route all extractions to human review instead.

explanation: A self-reported confidence value is just another generated token, not a calibrated probability — nothing makes items scoring 0.9 correct 90% of the time. Before routing on it, compare the scores against labeled ground truth, measure the real precision at each candidate cutoff, and set the threshold from that measurement (A).

distractors.B: Moving an uncalibrated number to a stricter value relocates an arbitrary line; without measured precision you still cannot say what auto-approval costs.
distractors.C: Miscalibration is not caused by context size — the score is a generated token either way, and a bigger window does not make it a probability.
distractors.D: Confidence routing works well once calibrated against labeled data; abandoning it throws away the main lever for safely cutting review volume.

stem: You have limited human-review capacity and want to spend it where it matters. Your extraction model can emit a confidence score per field. How should you use it to route review?

options.A: Calibrate the confidence scores against a labeled set, then route low-confidence and ambiguous items to review
options.B: Review a fixed random 10% sample of all extractions, ignoring the confidence scores entirely
options.C: Trust the raw confidence scores uncalibrated and send only extractions scoring below 0.5 to review
options.D: Review only the extractions the model scored most confidently, since those carry the highest value

explanation: Raw model confidence is often mis-calibrated, so calibrate the field-level scores against a labeled validation set first, then route the low-confidence and ambiguous or self-contradictory extractions to your reviewers (A). That concentrates scarce human attention where errors are most likely, which is the whole point of routing.

distractors.B: A blanket random sample ignores the signal you already have, spending review on easy cases and missing risky ones.
distractors.C: Uncalibrated scores can be systematically over- or under-confident, so a fixed 0.5 cutoff routes the wrong population.
distractors.D: Reviewing the most-confident extractions spends scarce capacity where errors are least likely — exactly backwards.

stem: A research agent has spent hours mapping a large repository. Its recent summaries describe components in generic terms and contradict details it had established earlier, and its transcript is now dominated by raw file dumps from the discovery phase. Which combination best addresses this?

options.A: Move the session to a model with a larger context window and carry on exploring exactly as before
options.B: Persist key findings to scratchpad files the agent re-reads, and run /compact when context fills
options.C: Restart the exploration in a fresh session whenever the agent's answers start to drift from earlier detail
options.D: Add a system-prompt instruction telling the agent to remember every established detail accurately

explanation: Context degradation in a long session is addressed on two fronts (B): offload key findings to scratchpad files the agent can re-read, so knowledge survives context pressure, and use /compact to shrink the accumulated raw file dumps. Together they reverse the drift toward generic "typical patterns" descriptions.

distractors.A: A bigger window delays degradation without preventing it, because the verbose discovery output keeps accumulating.
distractors.C: Restarting discards hours of mapping every time drift appears, and the same drift returns as the new session fills.
distractors.D: A prompt instruction to remember cannot overcome the mechanical degradation of an overloaded context.

stem: In your research system, two credible source subagents return different figures for the same metric, and a third pair of figures differ only because they are from different years. The synthesis agent currently picks one value and drops the rest, and sometimes flags year-over-year changes as "contradictions." What should the synthesis design do instead?

options.A: Average the conflicting figures into a single consensus value and report that
options.B: Keep the figure from whichever subagent responded first and discard the later ones
options.C: Drop any metric where sources disagree so the report contains only uncontested figures
options.D: Require each figure to carry its source and date, and surface unresolved conflicts rather than picking one

explanation: Preserving provenance is the fix (D): structured claim-source mappings — value, source URL or document, and publication or collection date — let synthesis annotate a real conflict with both sources instead of arbitrarily choosing one. The dates do the second job, separating a genuine disagreement from a legitimate year-over-year change so temporal differences are not reported as contradictions.

distractors.A: Averaging invents a value neither source supports and erases the provenance a reader would need to check either figure.
distractors.B: Response order says nothing about which figure is correct or better sourced; the slower subagent may have the better citation.
distractors.C: Dropping contested metrics discards real signal, and the year-over-year pair is not even in conflict — this suppresses correct data too.
